records.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
records.current_summary:
Subcarpathian (Podkarpackie) is the epicentre and last holdout of Poland's "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution wave. It was one of five voivodeships adopting a regional anti-LGBT declaration (repealed 20 September 2021 only after the European Commission threatened to freeze its regional development funds), and its Łańcut county held Poland's final surviving anti-LGBT charter of the family until its extraordinary-session repeal on 24 April 2025—six years after the phenomenon began. The capital, Rzeszów, saw its mayor Tadeusz Ferenc outright ban the 2019 Equality March on security grounds; the district court later overturned the ban and the march proceeded, but the executive intent to exclude a visible LGBTQ public presence is on the record.

The resolutions were never criminal statutes, but the repeal was extrinsic (EU funding leverage) rather than a change in local attitudes, meaning the de facto social climate that produced them persists. For a visitor, the practical exposure is being visibly trans at a public event in an eastern Podkarpackie town where the local authority resisted all external pressure until 2025.

Score of 0.42 sits 0.10 below the national 0.52. Well below Łódź (0.48), which also carried a voivodeship-level resolution but produced neither a march ban nor a five-year institutional holdout. This is the deepest sub-national negative in Poland's dossier.

sources.claim: Notes from Poland (27 Apr 2025): the county of Łańcut in southeast Poland (Podkarpackie) — the last local authority in the country with an anti-LGBT resolution — repealed the measure at an extraordinary councillors' session, closing the resolution era; at the wave's peak about one third of Poland's territory was covered by such documents (per the Atlas of Hate mapping project). Dated end-point for the record's 'last holdout' claim.

The Them (23 Sep 2021, updated 29 Sep): Podkarpackie's voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on Monday 20 September 2021, alongside Małopolska and Lubelskie — after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds; Podkarpackie replaced its ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. Confirms the record's 2021 voivodeship repeal under EU funding pressure.

freshness_all.fact: Podkarpackie's resolution revoked 27 Sep 2021; all such documents repealed/invalidated by 24 Apr 2025.
2019 court removal of the Rzeszów equality-march ban stands as recorded; no later Rzeszów ban found in searches.
Mayor's 2019 decision not to appeal the march-ban reversal stands as recorded fact.

records.name: Bauchi
records.current_summary:
Bauchi sits in the twelve-state Sharia criminal bloc of northern Nigeria, and it is where that system's ultimate penalty was actually pronounced: in June 2022 a Sharia court in Ningi sentenced three men — including a 70-year-old — to death by stoning for same-sex acts after arrest by the Hisbah religious police, reportedly the first time a death sentence has actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out; no execution is on record.

The appellate counterweight is real but fragile: the state's Upper Sharia Court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003 (denial of counsel, defective confession), and Amnesty International recorded a string of similar successful appeals. A June 2025 country-of-origin note confirms the code remains in force, and corporal enforcement of Sharia morality law in Bauchi continues to be cited in 2025–26 advisory material.
records.current_localsOnly: The stoning appeals that succeeded (Babaji 2003, Chiyawa 2003) were resident defendants represented by a Nigerian legal-aid group; the appellate check recorded by Amnesty operated on resident cases.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (Reuters returns 401 to automated fetches); the underlying Reuters report (2 July 2022) covers the Ningi Sharia court sentencing three men - a 70-year-old among them - to death by stoning for homosexuality after a 14 June 2022 Hisbah arrest, the first time the death penalty has actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria.

Amnesty International press release (2004): the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning 'sodomy' sentence (convicted 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001) for denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003 - 'a number of cases where convictions and sentences to death have been quashed on appeal'. Also records a then-pending stoning appeal (Usman/Ibrahim) before a Sharia Court of Appeal in Niger State.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note, June 2025, confirming the Sharia Penal Codes of the twelve northern states, including Bauchi, remain in force. The note records that a Sharia court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning for 'homosexual acts' in 2022 but that the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and that a further report placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in Bauchi in May 2024. It also records that at a sodomy trial in January 2014 at Bauchi's Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court an angry mob stormed the premises demanding a death sentence. This is the June 2025 government note the record cites for the code remaining in force and for the 2022 sentence having been pronounced but not executed.

sources.title: In Bauchi, 70-year-old Man, Two Others to Die by Stoning over Homosexuality - THISDAYLIVE
sources.claim: THISDAY, 3 July 2022: a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area of Bauchi State sentenced three men to death by stoning for homosexuality, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna, based on Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested committing the offence at Gwada village, Ningi LGA on 14 June 2022. Second national Nigerian paper confirming that Bauchi's Sharia court actually pronounced the stoning sentence this record is about.

sources.title: Homosexuality: How sharia court sentenced septuagenarian, others to death - Relatives | Punch Newspapers
sources.claim: Punch report of the 28 June 2022 Ningi Sharia Court death-by-stoning sentence against three men in Bauchi State, built on interviews with relatives, published 16 July 2022. It records that presiding Shariah judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi held the men violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001, that a 30-day appeal window was granted, and - through relatives of the convicted men - that the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. Confirms both the pronouncement of the sentence and the absence of any execution on record that the summary relies on.

freshness_all.fact: The July 2022 Bauchi stoning sentences did not stand: accused were released on bail pending appeal and no execution has occurred; sharia capital exposure nonetheless remains live (Aug 2026 UK advisory; 2025 Akwa Ibom case).

records.name: Kano
records.current_summary:
Kano is one of twelve northern Nigerian states running a parallel Sharia criminal code for Muslims: its Penal Code Law took effect 26 November 2000, prescribing 100 lashes plus up to a year's imprisonment for unmarried persons convicted of consensual same-sex activity and stoning to death for married or previously-married offenders. The state's Hisbah religious police are documented as the most active command among the three states studied in a 2019 rights-monitoring survey of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 — enforcement that operates alongside, not merely on paper beside, the secular police.

A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the Sharia codes remain in force and singles out Kano as one of only two states whose law carries a capital maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men. No trans-specific incident is on the state's record; the capital text plus the most active morality-police infrastructure is the finding.

sources.claim: Equaldex log entry #14124: the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000 took effect in Kano on 26 November 2000; consensual same-sex activity draws 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment if unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) if the offender is or has been married.

NOTE: document not retrievable at fetch time (403); the underlying USCIRF 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation uses 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara, and records Hisbah (religious police) activity in each, including Kano as the most active command.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note, June 2025, which singles out Kano among the twelve northern Sharia-code states. Its comparative table lists the Kano Sharia Penal Code (2000) as prescribing death by stoning for married or previously married men and 100 lashes with imprisonment for up to one year for unmarried men, and states that in Kano and Katsina the maximum penalty for 'lesbianism' is death while the other ten states punish it by flogging and up to six months' imprisonment. The note also records Kano-specific enforcement and gender-expression facts: eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on the premises of the hisbah in Kano state in 2023, and Kano's separate Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men. This is the June 2025 government note the record cites for the codes remaining in force and for Kano's capital maximum applying to same-sex acts between women as well as men.

freshness_all.fact: Kano's Sharia provisions remain in force (death by stoning for men, liti for women); a Sharia court death sentence (reported Jul 2022, Reuters) and 2024 arrest waves confirm live application.

newer.title: Equaldex log #14124: Homosexual activity in Kano

freshness_all.fact: Equaldex current-version entry (2024): homosexual activity in Kano illegal, death penalty as punishment, in force since Nov 2000; no change found since.
Sharia codes in force in Kano (named); death maximum for liwat; Kano one of two states where lesbianism also carries maximum death penalty.

records.name: Sokoto
records.current_summary:
Sokoto's Sharia Penal Code took effect 31 January 2001 within Nigeria's twelve-state religious-criminal bloc: male same-sex activity draws stoning to death for married or previously-married offenders and 100 lashes for the unmarried, and acts between women are punished by discretionary sentence of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases (2017) covers Sokoto among the three sample states, confirming operational religious courts and Hisbah activity there, and a June 2025 government note confirms the codes remain in force.

No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Sokoto — that record belongs to a neighbouring state — and no trans-specific incident is documented. The finding is capital-heavy statutory text combined with verified court-level enforcement.

sources.claim: Equaldex log entry #14118: the Sharia Penal Code Laws took effect in Sokoto on 31 January 2001; male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and 100 lashes otherwise; sexual acts between women (wsafa) draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment.

sources.title: Proceedings and Judgments in the Safiyatu Hussaini Case (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. V)
sources.claim: This chapter of the academic sourcebook reproduces the full record of a capital prosecution in Sokoto State's Sharia courts. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa (Sokoto State) convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. On her appeal, filed 26 October 2001, the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. For this record the document evidences that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the same capital-punishment framework (for zina, not same-sex conduct) the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

sources.title: Interim and Final Reports of the Committee Set Up to Advise the Sokoto State Government on the Establishment of Sharia (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. II)
sources.claim: Primary committee reports mapping Sokoto's Sharia adoption: the interim report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999 and the final report on 16 December 1999, with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts applying Sharia law in Sokoto State. They document the state-level groundwork for the Sokoto Sharia Penal Code - in force from 31 January 2001 per this record's other sources - that carries the stoning and lashing penalties for men's same-sex acts described in this record.

records.name: Yobe
records.current_summary:
Yobe is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states that extended religious law into criminal jurisdiction during the 1999–2002 wave, giving Sharia courts authority over Muslims for conduct beyond the federal criminal code. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the Sharia penal codes in these states — Yobe among them — remain in force, with the death penalty as the maximum for men's same-sex acts across all twelve and penalties for women ranging up to death in a minority of states; the same note's enforcement section records the 2023 public flogging of a person for cross-dressing, a trans-adjacent Sharia-police punishment.

Yobe's own dossier records no state-level court-case study and no further named incidents; the risk profile is the parallel criminal jurisdiction itself plus bloc-wide enforcement reporting, set against federal law that reaches only men's acts.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the twelve states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002 — the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on SOGIESC in Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025): the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct (up to 14 years, attempted 3 years) and is silent on women; Sharia penal codes in the 12 northern states apply to Muslims, with death the maximum for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death (in a minority of states) to flogging and imprisonment; the enforcement-and-Hisbah section records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023 and notes few secular cases reach court.

sources.title: Yobe State - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Reference article on Yobe State recording that the state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims and that Sharia law was established in the state in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim. For this record it confirms, in a jurisdiction-specific source, that Yobe adopted Sharia within the 1999-2002 wave that created the state's parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims.

records.name: Katsina
records.current_summary:
Katsina is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states that built a parallel Sharia criminal jurisdiction over Muslims in the 1999–2002 wave, documented in an international-rights organisation's chapter on the extension and in a June 2025 government country-of-origin note on the country's hybrid legal system. Its code stands out for reach: the same 2025 note records Katsina as one of only two states whose law carries the death penalty as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

No court-case study samples Katsina, no Hisbah operation is documented for it, and no trans-specific incident is on record; the elevated statutory reach over women's conduct is the differentiating fact, with the bloc-wide caveat that enforcement data are partial.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (2004) 'Nigeria: Unconsensual Sodomy Laws' chapter, fetched fresh this wave: documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria, explicitly listing the twelve states concerned — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law (promulgated 27 Oct 1999, in force 27 Jan 2000). Serves this record's northern-bloc criminalisation claim; freshness confirms the provisions still in force.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025): documents the hybrid legal system and the 12-state Sharia criminal layer, its coverage of women, and arrest-data limits. (Cache captured the front-matter only; content as catalogued in the research dossier.)

sources.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part III — The Sharia Penal Codes (Ostien, ed.)
sources.claim: Ostien's annotated volume lists Katsina's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, coming into operation on 20 June 2001 and gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23, 27 August 2001, and its annotation records Katsina among the three states (with Kaduna and Kebbi) whose sodomy text reads 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', while the lesbianism offence is punished by stoning to death - footnote 183 shows only Kano and Katsina reaching that capital maximum, against the harmonised code's base of 50 lashes and up to six months. Independent academic source for this record's claim that Katsina is one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

freshness_all.fact: Current source (Jun 2025): Katsina remains a Sharia-penal-code state with same-sex conduct criminalised; part of the northern twelve.
Sharia in force; death maximum for liwat; Katsina is one of only two states (with Kano) where 'lesbianism' also carries a maximum death penalty.

records.name: Kebbi
records.current_summary:
Kebbi runs Sharia criminal law as one of the twelve northern states that had adopted it by 2002, with Sharia courts exercising criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants in parallel with the federal system (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal penal code criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide, and the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that these twelve states' Sharia penal codes extend that criminalisation to same-sex acts between women, with a maximum of death for men and flogging or imprisonment for women.

No Kebbi-specific enforcement record against trans people exists; the case-level documentation of Sharia enforcement covers three other bloc states (USCIRF study, 2017). For a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor who is outed, the practical difference from the rest of the country is jurisdictional: exposure to a Sharia court applying a criminal code that is broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the federal statute alone.

sources.claim: HRW 2004 report, chapter IV 'The extension of Shari'a to criminal law': Zamfara first re-adopted criminal Shari'a (Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000); by 2002 twelve northern states - Kebbi among them - had Shari'a criminal legislation and Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, the only states with such jurisdiction.

sources.title: Nigeria: Sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics — Country Policy and Information Note (UK Home Office, June 2025)
sources.claim: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3): Kebbi's Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21) (2000) with death by stoning for liwat (sodomy) and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to 6 months for same-sex acts between women - the standard bloc penalty for women's conduct rather than the Kano/Katsina capital maximum. Dated government confirmation that Kebbi's Sharia layer extends criminalisation to acts between women, matching this record's claim that the state's code is broader in scope and harsher than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

sources.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part III — The Sharia Penal Codes (Ostien, ed.)
sources.claim: Ostien's annotated volume lists Kebbi's Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, Law No. 21 of 2000, signed into law and coming into operation on 1 December 2000 (Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000), and its annotations record Kebbi as one of three states (with Kaduna and Katsina) whose enacted text states 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', while lesbianism follows the harmonised code's 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment. Enactment-level confirmation that Kebbi adopted its own Sharia penal layer in the 1999-2002 wave with a capital ceiling for men's acts and women's same-sex conduct criminalised, grounding this record's jurisdictional-difference finding in Kebbi's own statute.

freshness_all.fact: No repeal in Kebbi since the 2019 mapping; Sharia criminal provisions plus the 2014 SSMPA remain in force.
Kebbi is among the 12 northern sharia-penal-code states criminalising same-sex acts (death maximum for men; flogging/imprisonment for women). No Kebbi-specific source in packet — group coverage only.

records.name: Niger
records.current_summary:
Niger State operates Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal anti-discrimination statute criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide; the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that the Sharia layer in these states extends criminalisation to acts between women.

No Kebbi-style state-specific enforcement or Hisbah record against trans people is documented for Niger; case-level enforcement records exist for other bloc states. The Sharia system adds a parallel criminal jurisdiction that the federation's southern states do not have, under which an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor faces broader charges and harsher penalties than under federal law alone.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (2004) 'Nigeria: Unconsensual Sodomy Laws' chapter, fetched fresh this wave: documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria, explicitly listing the twelve states concerned — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law (promulgated 27 Oct 1999, in force 27 Jan 2000). Serves this record's northern-bloc criminalisation claim; freshness confirms the provisions still in force.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025): documents the hybrid legal system and the 12-state Sharia criminal layer, its coverage of women, and arrest-data limits. (Cache captured the front-matter only; content as catalogued in the research dossier.)

sources.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part IV — The Niger State Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (Ostien, ed.)
sources.claim: Ostien's sourcebook reproduces Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 in full — a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36) and coming into force on 4 May 2000. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment (with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68), while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. State-level statutory proof that Niger, like the other northern bloc states, built a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants — the legal layer this record identifies as the visitor-facing risk beyond federal law.

sources.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part III — The Sharia Penal Codes (Ostien, ed.)
sources.claim: The annotated sourcebook catalogue records Niger: Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, HB.4/2000, signed into law on 22 February 2000 and coming into operation on 4 May 2000 (Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8, 9 March 2000). The editor notes it is not a complete Sharia Penal Code: it merely amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and it is printed in its entirety in Part IV of the same chapter. Confirms the state-specific enactment behind this record's claim that an outed Muslim visitor in Niger State stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

freshness_all.fact: Current source (Jun 2025): Niger State criminalisation unchanged under Sharia provisions applied since 1999-2000 plus the 2014 SSMPA.
Niger state is within the 12 northern sharia-penal-code states criminalising same-sex acts (death maximum for men); federal/state strands also criminalise; current per CPIN.
